name: Sereja and Sets
description: Let's assume that set S consists of m distinct intervals [ l 1 , r 1 ] , [ l 2 , r 2 ] , ... , [ l m , r m ] ( 1 ≤ l i ≤ r i ≤ n ; l i , r i are integers). Let's assume that f ( S ) is the maximum number of intervals that you can choose from the set S , such that every two of them do not intersect. We assume that two intervals, [ l 1 , r 1 ] and [ l 2 , r 2 ] , intersect if there is an integer x , which meets two inequalities: l 1 ≤ x ≤ r 1 and l 2 ≤ x ≤ r 2 . Sereja wonders, how many sets S are there, such that f ( S ) = k ? Count this number modulo 1000000007 (10 9 + 7) .
input_specification: The first line contains integers n , k (1 ≤ n ≤ 500; 0 ≤ k ≤ 500) .
output_specification: In a single line, print the answer to the problem modulo 1000000007 (10 9 + 7) .
subsubtopic: 461. Interval DP / Range DP / Matrix Chain Multiplication (MCM)
approach_summary: Iterate over interval length len from 1 to N and left endpoint l. Transition by splitting at midpoint k: dp[l][r] = min/max_k (dp[l][k] + dp[k+1][r] + cost) in O(N^3).

topic_editorial.summary: Interval / Range Dynamic Programming by interval length.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The problem satisfies interval substructure: the optimal cost for range $[l, r]$ depends on splitting into subsegments $[l, k]$ and $[k+1, r]$ for some pivot $k \in [l, r-1]$. Computing shorter intervals first ensures that all subproblems are ready when evaluating longer intervals.
